messages.content: I want to develop a learned large-eddy closure that reconciles local energy backscatter with long-horizon stability across unseen Reynolds numbers. The targets are a 20% reduction in kinetic-energy spectrum error relative to dynamic Smagorinsky on held-out Reynolds numbers, and bounded kinetic energy for 100 eddy-turnover times without suppressing all local backscatter.

Those targets put two distinct demands on the closure. It should represent the kinetic-energy spectrum more accurately than dynamic Smagorinsky on Reynolds numbers held out from development, while remaining stable over a long interval. The stability requirement does not call for eliminating backscatter: some local energy transfer back toward the resolved scales must remain possible.
What is the tension between backscatter and stability here?

Local backscatter means that, in some places or at some times, the closure permits energy transfer toward the resolved flow. That behavior is not the same as uncontrolled growth of the flow’s total kinetic energy. The challenge is to retain those local transfers while keeping kinetic energy bounded over the specified 100 eddy-turnover times.
So does bounded kinetic energy mean the energy has to decrease throughout the run?

No. Bounded kinetic energy does not mean monotonically decreasing kinetic energy, nor does it prohibit temporary increases. It means the energy must not run away over the 100-eddy-turnover-time horizon. The goal does not specify a numerical energy bound or require the energy to follow a particular time history.
And allowing backscatter does not mean the closure should add energy everywhere?

Right. The requirement concerns *local* backscatter, not energy addition everywhere or at every time. It leaves room for energy-transfer behavior that varies locally, while ruling out a solution that obtains stability simply by suppressing all local backscatter.
Could I satisfy the stability condition by making the learned closure entirely dissipative?

That might address one side of the stated tension, but it would not satisfy the full goal if it suppressed all local backscatter. The requested closure must combine bounded kinetic energy over 100 eddy-turnover times with the continued possibility of local backscatter.
How should I read the 20% figure?

It is a relative comparison of kinetic-energy spectrum error against dynamic Smagorinsky on held-out Reynolds numbers. Using the same error measure for both, a 20% reduction means an error no greater than 80% of the baseline error. The goal does not specify the detailed spectrum-error metric.
Is dynamic Smagorinsky the stability benchmark as well?

The explicit comparison to dynamic Smagorinsky is for kinetic-energy spectrum error. The other explicit target is that the learned closure maintain bounded kinetic energy for 100 eddy-turnover times without suppressing all local backscatter. No separate stability comparison with dynamic Smagorinsky is stated.
Why mention held-out Reynolds numbers rather than just spectrum accuracy?

Because the accuracy target concerns Reynolds numbers not used in developing the closure. The broader goal is to reconcile backscatter and long-horizon stability across unseen Reynolds numbers, rather than to obtain those properties only at a Reynolds number already encountered during development. No particular Reynolds-number values or ranges are specified.
Does the wording say how many Reynolds numbers must be held out?

No. It specifies held-out Reynolds numbers as the setting for the 20% spectrum-error comparison, but it gives neither a count nor particular values. Those details cannot be inferred from the target alone.
What does 100 eddy-turnover times add to the requirement?

It makes stability a long-horizon requirement, expressed in a flow-based time unit. The kinetic energy must remain bounded over that stated duration; a closure that behaves acceptably only for a much shorter interval would not establish the requested property. The duration is 100 eddy-turnover times, not an unspecified number of simulation steps.
Could a spectrum match at one instant establish the goal?

No. A spectrum-error result would address the accuracy comparison, but by itself would not show bounded kinetic energy through 100 eddy-turnover times or the preservation of some local backscatter. The goal asks for those properties together.
Likewise, would a bounded energy trace establish the spectrum target?

Not by itself. Bounded kinetic energy addresses the long-horizon condition, whereas the 20% target concerns kinetic-energy spectrum error relative to dynamic Smagorinsky on held-out Reynolds numbers. One does not automatically demonstrate the other.
When we say “learned large-eddy closure,” what are we committing to?

The phrase identifies a learned closure for large-eddy simulation: a model of effects not directly resolved in the simulated flow. It does not, on its own, select an architecture, inputs, training procedure, or particular numerical implementation. The commitments stated here are the behavior and evaluation targets for that closure.
Is the objective to maximize local backscatter, then?

No. The objective is not to maximize backscatter. It is to avoid suppressing *all* local backscatter while maintaining bounded kinetic energy. The statement gives no target amount, frequency, or spatial extent of backscatter.
I want to be careful about the word “reconcile.” What would it mean in this goal?

Here, “reconcile” means satisfying the apparently competing requirements within the same learned closure: permit local backscatter, yet maintain long-horizon kinetic-energy stability, including across unseen Reynolds numbers. It does not claim that either behavior has already been demonstrated.
Does “bounded” imply a precise tolerance around a reference energy?

No precise tolerance or reference-energy band is supplied. The stated requirement is bounded kinetic energy for 100 eddy-turnover times. A concrete assessment would need to make the meaning of an acceptable bound clear, but the goal itself does not give a numerical threshold.
Then I should avoid treating a low spectrum error as permission to ignore a slow energy drift?

Yes. The spectrum-error comparison and the 100-eddy-turnover-time energy condition are separate requirements. Meeting the 20% relative spectrum-error target would not excuse kinetic energy that fails to remain bounded over the required horizon.
And I should not claim success merely because the kinetic energy remains bounded after removing every instance of backscatter?

Correct. The stability condition explicitly includes “without suppressing all local backscatter.” An entirely backscatter-free result would leave that part of the goal unmet, even if kinetic energy remained bounded for 100 eddy-turnover times.
Can you put the full goal in one precise sentence without adding a method?

Develop a learned large-eddy closure that allows some local energy backscatter while maintaining bounded kinetic energy for 100 eddy-turnover times across unseen Reynolds numbers, and reduces kinetic-energy spectrum error by 20% relative to dynamic Smagorinsky on held-out Reynolds numbers.
That keeps the accuracy comparison separate from the long-horizon condition. Does it also leave open how those outcomes are achieved?

Yes. It states the desired outcomes and the specified comparison without claiming an architecture, mechanism, experiment, or completed result. In particular, it does not assume that preserving backscatter alone improves the spectrum, or that a lower spectrum error alone guarantees stable long-horizon behavior.

For the learned large-eddy closure, I propose training a Galilean-invariant neural subgrid-scale (SGS) stress with spectrum and rollout losses, plus an energy-dependent net-dissipation projection that preserves local backscatter.

That is a proposed way to address the two sides of the goal together. The neural SGS stress would provide the learned closure. The spectrum loss would address spectral fidelity, while the rollout loss would address behavior over time. The energy-dependent net-dissipation projection would constrain the overall energy-transfer behavior without requiring every local transfer to be dissipative. None of those choices, by itself, establishes the stated accuracy or stability targets.
What exactly does Galilean-invariant mean in this proposal?

It means the learned SGS stress should behave consistently if a constant velocity is added to the entire flow—a change of inertial reference frame. The closure should not depend spuriously on that uniform shift. The proposal specifies Galilean invariance, but does not specify the model inputs, architecture, or means of enforcing it.
Does calling it Galilean-invariant also commit us to every other symmetry?
No. Galilean invariance is the stated property. It does not, by itself, establish rotation invariance, reflection symmetry, or any other property that the proposal has not specified.
Why specify a neural SGS stress rather than simply saying “a neural closure”?

It identifies what the learned component is meant to provide: a subgrid-scale stress for the large-eddy model. “Neural closure” alone would leave that less clear. The proposal still does not prescribe a particular neural network or a particular form for the stress.
How do the two losses divide the work?

The spectrum loss is directed at discrepancies in the kinetic-energy spectrum; the rollout loss is directed at behavior during a time-evolving simulation. Using both expresses the intent to consider spectral accuracy and evolving behavior during training, rather than treating either one as a complete substitute for the other. The proposal does not state their formulas or relative weights.
Is a rollout loss the same thing as proving stability for 100 eddy-turnover times?

No. It is a training objective related to time-evolving behavior, not a proof that kinetic energy will remain bounded for 100 eddy-turnover times. The proposal does not specify a rollout length, and the long-horizon requirement would still need to be assessed.
Likewise, does adding a spectrum loss guarantee the 20% improvement over dynamic Smagorinsky?

No. It makes spectrum fidelity part of the training objective, but the 20% reduction in kinetic-energy spectrum error relative to dynamic Smagorinsky on held-out Reynolds numbers remains a target, not a reported result. A training loss is not itself the held-out comparison.
I want to understand the projection. Is it supposed to eliminate any backscatter the neural stress produces?

No. The proposal explicitly says the energy-dependent net-dissipation projection preserves local backscatter. Its stated role concerns *net* dissipation, rather than forcing dissipation at every location. That distinction is essential: local transfers toward resolved energy may remain even while an overall energy-transfer constraint is applied.
So “net” refers to an aggregate rather than a pointwise ban on energy input?

Yes, that is the conceptual distinction in the proposal. A pointwise ban on energy input would suppress local backscatter. A net-dissipation projection is intended to constrain the combined effect while leaving room for local backscatter. The proposal does not say precisely how the aggregate is calculated or how the projection is implemented.
What makes the projection energy-dependent?

Its action is proposed to depend on energy, rather than being an unchanging constraint applied without regard to energy. The node does not specify which energy quantity it uses, how that dependence is expressed, or when the projection acts. Those are open implementation details, not facts to assume.
Should I picture the projection as overriding the trained stress everywhere?

That would be more specific than the proposal allows, and overriding it everywhere in a way that removes all backscatter would conflict with its stated purpose. What is specified is a projection for net dissipation that preserves local backscatter; its detailed effect on individual stress predictions is not given.
Does preserving local backscatter mean guaranteeing it at every time?

No such guarantee is stated. Preserving local backscatter means the proposed projection is not intended to rule it out altogether. The proposal sets no required frequency, magnitude, or location for backscatter.
Could the projection alone be described as the stability solution?

It is a proposed stability-oriented component, but calling it a demonstrated solution would go beyond the proposal. Whether the complete closure maintains bounded kinetic energy for 100 eddy-turnover times, while retaining local backscatter, remains to be established.
How do the losses and projection fit together without treating them as interchangeable?

They have different stated roles. Spectrum and rollout losses guide training of the Galilean-invariant neural SGS stress; the energy-dependent net-dissipation projection constrains the resulting energy-transfer behavior while preserving local backscatter. A spectrum loss is not a net-dissipation constraint, and a net-dissipation constraint is not a substitute for checking spectrum error.
Does this proposal say which Reynolds numbers appear in training or how generalization is measured?

No. The goal calls for performance on held-out or unseen Reynolds numbers, but this proposal does not specify particular Reynolds numbers, a training split, or an evaluation procedure. It identifies a candidate approach to the goal, not a completed generalization result.
Would it be accurate to say the projection guarantees bounded kinetic energy simply because it is energy-dependent?

No. Energy dependence describes a feature of the proposed projection; it does not establish a guarantee. In particular, the proposal supplies neither a mathematical bound nor a demonstrated 100-eddy-turnover-time rollout. Those would not follow merely from the phrase “energy-dependent.”
What if someone reads “net dissipation” as “no positive local energy transfer is allowed”?

That would erase the distinction the proposal makes. Net dissipation concerns the combined transfer, whereas local backscatter concerns transfers in particular places or times. The projection is expressly intended to preserve local backscatter, not prohibit every positive local transfer.
Can we state the proposal concisely without implying that it has already worked?

Propose training a Galilean-invariant neural SGS stress using spectrum and rollout losses, together with an energy-dependent net-dissipation projection designed to preserve local backscatter. This describes the intended approach; it does not claim a 20% held-out spectrum-error reduction or bounded kinetic energy over 100 eddy-turnover times has been achieved.
And the main unresolved question is whether that combination actually delivers both targets on unseen Reynolds numbers?

Yes. The proposal brings spectral training, time-evolving training, and a backscatter-preserving net-dissipation constraint into one approach. Whether that approach reduces kinetic-energy spectrum error by 20% relative to dynamic Smagorinsky on held-out Reynolds numbers *and* maintains bounded kinetic energy for 100 eddy-turnover times without suppressing all local backscatter remains an outcome to establish.
Can the net-dissipation projection bound kinetic energy for 100 eddy-turnover times at unseen Reynolds numbers while retaining local backscatter?

That is the open question. A net-dissipation projection is intended to constrain the combined energy transfer without prohibiting local backscatter, so the two requirements are not logically incompatible. But the projection’s description alone does not establish bounded kinetic energy for 100 eddy-turnover times at unseen Reynolds numbers, or show how much local backscatter remains.
Why aren’t net dissipation and local backscatter contradictory?

They describe different levels of behavior. Local backscatter is energy transfer toward the resolved flow in a particular region or at a particular time. Net dissipation concerns the combined effect of transfers. Some local transfers can point toward the resolved flow even if the combined effect is dissipative.
Then if the projection enforces net dissipation, is bounded kinetic energy automatic?

Not from that description alone. A constraint on the closure’s net energy transfer is not, by itself, a stated bound on the kinetic energy of the evolving flow for 100 eddy-turnover times. The projection’s exact constraint and its relationship to the full energy evolution are not specified here.
Is the 100-eddy-turnover-time part asking about a single instant at the end?

No. The question is whether kinetic energy remains bounded over the 100-eddy-turnover-time horizon, not merely whether it has an acceptable value at the endpoint. It concerns the evolving behavior throughout that interval.
Does bounded energy mean there can be no temporary rise when backscatter occurs?

No. Boundedness does not require kinetic energy to decrease at every moment. Temporary increases, including ones associated with local backscatter, are not inherently inconsistent with remaining bounded across the stated horizon.
What exactly has to be retained for us to say local backscatter remains?

There must still be some local transfer toward the resolved flow, rather than a projection that eliminates all such transfers. The question does not specify a required magnitude, frequency, or location of backscatter, so it does not support a more precise threshold.
Could the net behavior be dissipative while local transfers change direction from place to place?

Conceptually, yes. A net condition can concern the aggregate while allowing individual local contributions of either sign. Whether the proposed projection actually has that behavior in an evolving closure is part of the question, not an observed result.
Why does the question specify unseen Reynolds numbers?

Because it asks whether the proposed balance between bounded energy and retained backscatter extends beyond Reynolds numbers encountered during development. Behavior at an unseen Reynolds number cannot simply be inferred from the projection’s name or from behavior at a Reynolds number already encountered.
Do we know which unseen Reynolds numbers are meant?
No particular values or range are given. The condition is general: the question concerns unseen Reynolds numbers, without specifying which ones or how many.
Could bounded energy at one unseen Reynolds number answer the question for all unseen Reynolds numbers?

It would address the Reynolds number examined, but it would not by itself establish behavior across unseen Reynolds numbers generally. The scope of any conclusion would have to match the Reynolds numbers and time horizons for which the behavior was actually established.
Is there a difference between asking whether the projection permits bounded behavior and asking whether it guarantees it?

Yes. The behavior might be possible with such a projection without following as a guarantee from its description. A guarantee would require enough detail to connect the projection to a bound on the evolving kinetic energy. The question supplies no such derivation or reported long-horizon result.
Would a mathematical net-dissipation condition, by itself, settle the local-backscatter part?

Not necessarily. A net condition tells us about an aggregate; it does not, without further information, tell us whether positive local transfers remain or have all been removed. Both the bounded-energy behavior and the preservation of local backscatter matter to this question.
Suppose the energy stayed bounded but the projection removed every local backscatter event. Would that answer yes?

No. The question asks whether it can bound kinetic energy for 100 eddy-turnover times at unseen Reynolds numbers *while retaining local backscatter*. Bounded energy obtained by eliminating all local backscatter would not meet that combined condition.
And what if local backscatter remained but energy grew without bound before 100 eddy-turnover times?
That would not meet the combined condition either. Retaining local backscatter does not substitute for bounded kinetic energy over the full 100-eddy-turnover-time horizon.
Does the word “projection” tell us precisely how strongly it changes the neural SGS stress?

No. It identifies a proposed constraining operation, but the question does not specify its formula or how much it alters any particular stress prediction. We therefore cannot infer the detailed local transfers or the long-horizon energy behavior from the word alone.
And does “energy-dependent” tell us when it acts?

Not precisely. It says the proposed projection depends on energy, but it does not state the energy quantity used, the form of that dependence, or the circumstances in which the projection changes the stress. Those details would matter to a stronger claim about boundedness.
Is this question about the spectrum-error target too?

Its focus is narrower: whether the net-dissipation projection can keep kinetic energy bounded for 100 eddy-turnover times at unseen Reynolds numbers while retaining local backscatter. The separate kinetic-energy spectrum-error target is not resolved by an answer about this projection’s energy behavior.
What is the most careful answer we can give right now?

The intended net constraint and local backscatter are conceptually compatible, but it remains undetermined whether this projection yields bounded kinetic energy throughout 100 eddy-turnover times at unseen Reynolds numbers while actually retaining local backscatter. The question states the behavior to establish; it does not report that behavior.

Here is a hypothesis for the projection: when energy is above 1.5× the training-set mean energy, enforce net SGS dissipation ≥ forcing power. I think that could bound kinetic energy for 100 eddy-turnover times while preserving local backscatter.

That is a specific hypothesis about how an energy-dependent net-dissipation projection might address the open question. Above the stated energy threshold, the proposed constraint makes net subgrid-scale (SGS) dissipation at least as large as forcing power. The hoped-for outcome is bounded kinetic energy over 100 eddy-turnover times without eliminating local backscatter. The constraint and the hoped-for outcome should be kept distinct: the latter has not been established by stating the former.
Can you spell out exactly when the inequality would apply?

As phrased, it applies when energy is *above* 1.5× the training-set mean energy. The hypothesis does not specify that this inequality must be enforced below that threshold, or exactly at it. It also does not specify the detailed energy measure used to trigger the projection.
Is 1.5× the training-set mean energy the bound I am claiming kinetic energy will never exceed?

No. In the hypothesis, 1.5× the training-set mean energy is the threshold above which the net-dissipation constraint is imposed. It is not stated as an absolute ceiling that kinetic energy can never cross. In fact, the stated condition is triggered by energy being above that level.
So the number is not 1.5 times the highest energy seen in training?
Correct. The reference is the *training-set mean energy*, not the training-set maximum. The hypothesis gives a multiplier of 1.5 and does not supply a numerical value for that mean energy.
What does the inequality mean in words?

When energy exceeds the stated threshold, the proposed projection would require the net SGS dissipation to be greater than or equal to the forcing power. Equality is allowed by “≥”; the hypothesis does not demand strictly greater dissipation.
Why compare dissipation with forcing power?

The comparison expresses the proposed high-energy response: when energy is above the threshold, the net SGS dissipation should at least match the power associated with forcing. That gives the hypothesis a concrete energy-budget rationale. Whether it suffices to bound the kinetic energy of the evolving flow for 100 eddy-turnover times is still the question, not a consequence we can assume.
Does net SGS dissipation ≥ forcing power prove that the total kinetic energy must decrease whenever the threshold is crossed?

Not from the information given. The inequality compares the specified net SGS contribution with forcing power, but the hypothesis does not provide a complete energy balance or a derivation of the total kinetic-energy evolution. It would be too strong to turn the proposed inequality alone into a proof of decreasing energy whenever the threshold is crossed.
But the hypothesis is that this condition bounds energy over the whole horizon?

Yes. The hypothesized outcome is bounded kinetic energy over 100 eddy-turnover times while local backscatter remains possible. The condition above 1.5× the training-set mean energy is the proposed means of achieving that outcome, not an already demonstrated 100-turnover bound.
Does the inequality also apply point by point, wherever there is backscatter?

No pointwise inequality is stated. The hypothesis says *net* SGS dissipation must be at least forcing power when the energy threshold is exceeded. A net constraint can leave room for local transfers toward resolved energy, which is why retaining local backscatter is part of the hypothesis.
Would local backscatter violate the high-energy rule?

Not necessarily. A local backscatter event and a net dissipative effect describe different things. The hypothesis allows for local backscatter while requiring the overall SGS dissipation to meet the forcing-power comparison above the threshold. Whether a particular projection can satisfy both is not established here.
If the net dissipation exactly equals forcing power, must every local SGS transfer be zero?

No. Equality of two net quantities does not require every local contribution to vanish. Local contributions can differ in sign and still have an aggregate that satisfies an equality. The hypothesis does not specify the local pattern or amount of backscatter.
Should I describe the rule as making the closure dissipative at every energy level?

No. The proposed inequality is conditional: it is stated for energy *above* 1.5× the training-set mean energy. Nor does its net character mean every local transfer must be dissipative when it applies. Describing it as unconditional, pointwise dissipation would change the hypothesis.
What happens below that threshold under this hypothesis?

The hypothesis does not say. It specifies the net-dissipation inequality above the threshold, but it does not prescribe a separate rule for energy below it. We should not fill in that missing behavior as if it had been decided.
Is the threshold itself measured in eddy-turnover times?

No. The threshold, 1.5× the training-set mean energy, is an energy level. The 100 eddy-turnover times specify how long kinetic energy is hypothesized to remain bounded. They are different quantities serving different roles.
Does the hypothesis say what numerical upper bound applies throughout those 100 eddy-turnover times?

It does not give a numerical upper bound for kinetic energy. It proposes a trigger level for the projection and hypothesizes bounded energy over the stated duration. The trigger level should not be silently substituted for a proven upper bound.
Does it say the projection must prevent every temporary energy increase?

No. The claim is bounded energy over the 100-eddy-turnover-time horizon, not monotonically decreasing energy. Temporary increases are not ruled out by the wording, and the intended preservation of local backscatter is consistent with allowing local transfer toward the resolved flow.
How does this connect to the question about unseen Reynolds numbers?

The preceding question asks whether the projection can deliver bounded kinetic energy for 100 eddy-turnover times at unseen Reynolds numbers while retaining local backscatter. This hypothesis offers a particular conditional inequality as a possible way to do that. It does not report that the inequality has achieved those properties at any unseen Reynolds number.
Would the same 1.5× threshold automatically have the same effect at every unseen Reynolds number?

That cannot be concluded from the hypothesis alone. It specifies the threshold relative to the training-set mean energy and the intended 100-turnover outcome, but gives no result establishing how the condition behaves across unseen Reynolds numbers.
Is the training-set mean energy a measured result we know numerically here?
No numerical mean is supplied. “Training-set mean energy” identifies the reference used by the proposed threshold; the dialogue does not establish its value or how it is calculated.
Can I call this a guarantee if I write the inequality into the projection?

Not on the basis of the hypothesis alone. Enforcing the stated inequality above the threshold would establish that particular conditional property of the projection, assuming it is enforced as stated. It would not, without further justification, establish bounded kinetic energy for 100 eddy-turnover times or demonstrate that local backscatter survives.
Then what is the careful one-sentence version of the hypothesis?

The hypothesis is that enforcing net SGS dissipation ≥ forcing power whenever energy is above 1.5× the training-set mean energy will keep kinetic energy bounded for 100 eddy-turnover times while preserving local backscatter.
And that leaves the proposed inequality, the duration, and the backscatter condition intact without claiming a result?

Yes. It states a proposed conditional mechanism and the behavior it is hypothesized to produce. It does not say that the 100-eddy-turnover-time bound has been demonstrated, that the threshold is an absolute energy ceiling, or that local backscatter has already been observed under the projection.

I plan to train projected and unprojected closures at Reλ=80 and 120, then test them at Reλ=160 and 200 over 100 eddy-turnover times. I’ll compare energy maxima, backscatter frequency, and spectral error.

That plan directly examines the question of whether the projection helps keep kinetic energy bounded while retaining local backscatter at unseen Reynolds numbers. Reλ=80 and 120 are the training conditions; Reλ=160 and 200 are the test conditions. Comparing projected with unprojected closures over 100 eddy-turnover times gives the energy and backscatter behavior a common stated horizon. This is a planned comparison, not a reported outcome.
Why include both projected and unprojected closures?

Their comparison is intended to show what differs when the projection is present. Energy maxima can speak to the magnitude of kinetic-energy excursions; backscatter frequency can speak to whether local backscatter remains; and spectral error can reveal differences in spectrum accuracy. The plan does not presume which closure will perform better on any of those measures.
Am I training at all four Reynolds numbers?

No. The plan specifies training the projected and unprojected closures at Reλ=80 and 120, and testing them at Reλ=160 and 200. Calling 160 and 200 test Reynolds numbers preserves the intended distinction.
Does “unseen” apply to both Reλ=160 and Reλ=200 here?

Yes, relative to the training conditions stated in this plan. Neither Reλ=160 nor Reλ=200 is listed as a training Reynolds number. The plan does not describe any other training conditions beyond Reλ=80 and 120.
Why test at two Reynolds numbers instead of talking about one unseen case?

The plan calls for both Reλ=160 and 200, so the comparison can be read separately at each of those test conditions. It would be premature to infer from the plan that their outcomes will agree, or that testing those two values establishes behavior at every unseen Reynolds number.
What should I take “over 100 turnovers” to mean in this plan?

It specifies the duration of the tests: 100 eddy-turnover times. The energy and backscatter question concerns behavior over that horizon, not just a short rollout or a reading at its endpoint. The plan does not provide a simulation-step count or another time unit.
Why compare energy maxima rather than only checking the final kinetic energy?

An energy maximum concerns the highest kinetic energy reached over the interval being examined. A final value alone could miss a larger excursion earlier in the 100-eddy-turnover-time test. Comparing maxima is therefore relevant to the bounded-energy question, although a maximum from one finite test is not, by itself, a general mathematical guarantee of boundedness.
Does the plan give an acceptable maximum energy?
No. It says to compare energy maxima but gives no numerical acceptance threshold for them. It also does not say that either closure has already met the bounded-energy requirement.
Would an energy maximum tell me whether the closure retained local backscatter?

Not on its own. Energy maxima describe an aspect of the overall kinetic-energy history. Backscatter frequency is the planned comparison that addresses how often local backscatter occurs. Keeping those observations separate matters because bounded energy could coexist with retained backscatter—or with its complete suppression.
What does backscatter frequency add to a simple yes-or-no observation of backscatter?

It provides a way to compare how often local backscatter occurs in the projected and unprojected tests, rather than recording only whether it appears at least once. The plan does not define the counting rule or specify a target frequency, so no particular numerical interpretation should be assumed.
If the projected closure has less frequent backscatter, must that mean the plan has failed?

Not necessarily. The stated concern is retaining local backscatter, not requiring the projected and unprojected closures to have identical backscatter frequencies. The comparison would make a difference visible; whether backscatter has been suppressed altogether is a distinct question. The plan supplies no minimum acceptable frequency.
What if its backscatter frequency is zero?

If a test found no local backscatter under the projected closure, that observation would be directly relevant to the requirement not to suppress all local backscatter. But the plan does not report such a finding, and the meaning of a measured frequency would depend on how it is defined and observed.
Why retain spectral error in a test focused on stability and backscatter?

The closure’s aim also includes kinetic-energy spectrum accuracy. Comparing spectral error alongside energy maxima and backscatter frequency prevents the projected-versus-unprojected comparison from considering only energy behavior. The plan does not specify a spectral-error formula or report an error value.
Does this plan itself specify a comparison against dynamic Smagorinsky?

No. This plan explicitly compares projected and unprojected closures using energy maxima, backscatter frequency, and spectral error at the stated Reynolds numbers and horizon. The broader goal names dynamic Smagorinsky as the baseline for a 20% kinetic-energy spectrum-error reduction on held-out Reynolds numbers, but that baseline comparison is not explicitly included in this plan.
So projected versus unprojected spectral error and the 20% baseline target are not automatically the same comparison?

Correct. A spectral-error comparison between the two closures could show how projection relates to spectral accuracy, but it would not automatically establish a 20% reduction relative to dynamic Smagorinsky. Those are different comparisons, and the plan states only the projected-versus-unprojected one.
Does “train projected and unprojected closures” specify whether their neural networks are identical?

No. It identifies the two kinds of closures to train and compare, but does not state their architectures or which other aspects of training are shared. We should not present those details as decisions already contained in the plan.
Can I say this is designed to isolate the projection’s effect?

You can say the projected-versus-unprojected comparison is intended to examine the projection’s contribution. A strong claim that any measured difference is attributable solely to the projection would require details about how the two closures are made comparable; this plan does not provide those details.
Does the plan specify how to measure backscatter frequency?

No. It names backscatter frequency as an outcome to compare, but leaves its measurement definition open. The important stated point is that the comparison should address local backscatter as well as energy maxima and spectral error.
And is “spectral error” necessarily a single error over the entire 100-turnover interval?

The plan does not say how spectral error is aggregated in time, or give its precise definition. It says to compare spectral error in tests over 100 turnovers. A specific aggregation rule would be an additional detail, not something established by the wording.
Could a lower energy maximum alone answer whether the projection achieves what we want?

No. It would be relevant to the energy side of the question, but the comparison also needs to account for whether local backscatter remains. Spectral error is another planned outcome. Moreover, a lower maximum than the unprojected closure would be a relative observation, not automatically proof of bounded energy across unseen Reynolds numbers generally.
If the projected closure performed differently at Reλ=160 and Reλ=200, should I collapse that into one verdict?

The plan specifies both test Reynolds numbers, so their outcomes should not be assumed identical or reduced to an unsupported general claim. A comparison at each would show what happened under that test condition; the plan itself supplies no result at either one.
Does observing bounded energy for 100 turnovers establish stability beyond that horizon?
No. The planned horizon is 100 eddy-turnover times. An observation over that interval would address that interval; it would not, without further support, establish behavior for longer times.
Can you restate the plan without making it sound as though the tests have already been run?

Train projected and unprojected closures at Reλ=80 and 120; test both at Reλ=160 and 200 for 100 eddy-turnover times; and compare their energy maxima, backscatter frequency, and spectral error. Those comparisons are planned to inform the bounded-energy and retained-backscatter question, not to announce its answer.

The activity now is to run 100-eddy-turnover-time large-eddy simulations (LES) at Reλ=160 and 200 with the projected and unprojected closures, and measure energy exceedances, local backscatter frequency, and spectral error.

That sets out the LES comparison to perform: use both closures at Reλ=160 and 200 over the stated 100-eddy-turnover-time horizon, then measure all three outcomes. Energy exceedances address the kinetic-energy behavior, local backscatter frequency addresses whether backscatter remains present, and spectral error addresses spectrum accuracy.
